Campaign brief: You can have an agent answering handbook and policy questions in Slack from your own documents — configured in a console rather than assembled from Slack events, a vector store and a model API — and you can test it on your real docs before you spend anything.
events.reader:
Selected audience: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs.
Situation context (grounded; check applicability): This is an ops/IT-adjacent person at a company where policies and handbooks are written up in Notion or similar docs and employees communicate primarily in Slack; when someone can't find an answer, they ping this person (or the team channel) directly, and this person has been asked to build or is considering building an automated Slack responder that draws on the Handbook, Docs, and Issue Trackers.
events.reader_segment: Ops or IT generalist standing up an internal Slack answer-bot over company docs
events.promise: You can have an agent answering handbook and policy questions in Slack from your own documents — configured in a console rather than assembled from Slack events, a vector store and a model API — and you can test it on your real docs before you spend anything.
events.arc: Single email, so the arc happens inside it: open on the question that keeps landing in Slack and the documentation it is buried in, name what orqAgent now makes available (an agent over your own documents, answering in a Slack channel, with no vector store to stand up), concede that the only honest way to judge the answers is on their own policy files, and close on the free, no-card start. The reader should finish knowing what the product is, that it is available now, and what the first ten minutes of trying it look like.

emails.job: Get an ops/IT generalist to sign up free and point one agent at their own handbook documents with Slack connected, so they judge it on their own questions rather than on our description of it.
emails.single_idea: The Slack answer-bot over your company documents is now something you configure rather than something you build: upload or connect your handbook files, install the Slack app, and the agent answers in the channel — with no vector store for you to stand up and run.
emails.objection: If I put this in the channel, who keeps it running afterwards — is this one more internal pipeline with no owner?
must_not_say: No plan numbers beyond $0, $29/month and the 1,500 signup credits — the published pricing pages disagree with each other on agent counts, executions and runs, and quoting a contradicted figure is a trust problem, not a detail.

No compliance or certification language of any kind: no SOC 2, no GDPR, no 'enterprise-ready', no security posture. This reader is not running a vendor review yet and the certification does not exist.
No uptime or SLA figure — the guarantee is Enterprise-only and the email is not selling Enterprise.
No guardrail claims (PII masking, content filtering, prompt-injection detection) — off limits for this campaign.

Do not describe it as a knowledge base product, a RAG platform or semantic search, and do not claim it will understand questions phrased differently from the documents. Describe only the documented behaviour — it matches the question against your documents and puts the best-matching passages in front of the model — and invite the reader to test it.
No competitor names and no comparison on speed, breadth, quality, effort, control, security or track record. The field is ahead of us on every one of those axes; raising them loses the email.
No customer names, quotes, logos, user counts or 'teams like yours' — none exist in the material, and inventing social proof is the fastest way to lose this reader.

Do not assume this person has already built a bot, runs an n8n stack, pays for a workspace AI assistant, has lost weeks to maintenance, or is about to leave the company. Their situation is a growing pile of docs and questions in Slack; anything beyond that is conditional at most.
No setup duration, migration time or 'in minutes' claim in this email — that number is not assigned here, and a first-call time would not prove a rollout time anyway.
No per-seat cost comparison, no savings figure, no claim about what this replaces on the invoice.
Do not promise it replaces the documentation, the helpdesk, or any part of the company's backend or workflow.
No hype vocabulary: not 'revolutionary', 'game-changing', 'cutting-edge', 'leverage', 'synergy', or 'solution' as a noun.
Do not promise voice or telephony support unless a current licensed source explicitly establishes it.
Do not claim that the agent layer replaces a company's complete backend, product UI, billing, or operational workflow without direct evidence.
Compliance and certification claims are unavailable unless the Evidence Ledger explicitly licenses them.
Do not claim Knowledge base / RAG context; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Agent guardrails; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Reusable per-client agent configuration; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Voice and telephony runtime; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim Full SaaS backend replacement; its capability state is unsupported.
Do not claim HIPAA compliance; its capability state is unknown.
Do not claim Deep domain-specific operational integrations; its capability state is unknown.

Retrieval is keyword scoring over roughly 500-token chunks (E56, E57) rather than semantic search, and the free tier caps the knowledge base at five documents (E120), so a question worded unlike the handbook or spread across a large page.
emails.felt_need: The same policy and handbook questions get asked repeatedly in Slack, and the answers are buried in documentation that is difficult to navigate.
emails.status_quo: Team members search Notion by trying random keywords or guessing document titles rather than getting a direct answer.
emails.why_it_fails: Manual search degrades as the documentation grows — past a couple of hundred pages, guessing at titles is what people actually do. And practitioners who take the low-code wiring route say plainly it is not the right fit for latency-sensitive, high-reliability production use or for deep observability: it gets a bot answering, and it leaves you owning a pipeline.
emails.mechanism: The agent is configured in a console instead of assembled: you write the system prompt, pick the model, and load your policy documents (.pdf, .txt, .markdown, .csv). On every call the platform matches the question against your documents and injects the top-scoring passages into the prompt, so the retrieval layer is part of the product rather than a vector database you run. Slack is an OAuth install — the bot replies to mentions and channel messages — and the agent answers from the documents you gave it, citing specific facts from them.

The policy question lands in the channel again, and the answer is in the handbook somewhere.

Usually that means someone searches the docs by hand — guessing at titles until the right page turns up — then pastes the paragraph back into Slack.

orqAgent is a no-code console for building AI agents, and the Slack answer-bot over your own documents is available in it today. Upload your policy files — PDFs, docs or plain text — and the agent retrieves the most relevant context for every question.

Connecting Slack is an OAuth install. The bot replies to mentions and channel messages, answering from the documents you gave it. **No vector DB to manage**, so there is no pipeline left behind for someone to own.

> **1,500 free credits** — no card required, so you can run it against your real handbook before anyone commits to anything.

The usual way to stop answering the same policy question in Slack is to build the bot that answers it.

That route is Slack events, a vector store and a model API wired together. Once it is replying in the channel, it is a pipeline someone owns — and the store behind it stays yours to keep running.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and that bot is now something you configure in it: write the system prompt, pick the model, and upload your handbook files as the agent's knowledge base.

The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage. Slack is an OAuth install, and the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

Every answer in the channel is a real run: it consumes credits and appears in Analytics exactly like an API call.

> **Starter costs $0** — 1,500 free credits, no card required. Point an agent at your own handbook and ask it the questions your team actually asks.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and it is available now. The answer-bot is something you configure there rather than assemble: write the system prompt, pick the model, upload your handbook files.

edits.line: Every answer in the channel is a real run: it consumes credits and appears in Analytics exactly like an API call.
edits.problem: This is the one idea the brief assigned the email, and it is written as a cost warning rather than as visibility: all three cold readers stopped reading at exactly this sentence, and two of them named it as the line they would cut because it introduces a spend mechanic with no number and answers nothing. edits.fix: Rebuild this beat so the logged run is the benefit, not the caveat: what the reader gets to see after each channel answer and why that matters when a bot is answering for the whole company. Keep it inside the licensed scope of E97 — runs consume credits and appear in Analytics like API calls — and do not attach a per-answer price or a credits-to-questions conversion, which the brief deliberately withholds. Place it where it lands as the point of the email, not as a footnote before the price.

edits.line: Once it is replying in the channel, it is a pipeline someone owns — and the store behind it stays yours to keep running.
edits.problem: The email raises ownership as the reason not to build, then never says who owns the orqAgent version. All three readers landed on the same gap — this is pitched as another no-code layer against a documented worry that low-code tooling does not hold up for always-on production use — and the draft answers it only by negation ("no vector DB to manage"). The objection the brief assigned to this email goes unkilled.
edits.fix: Answer the ownership question positively with what the evidence licenses: E9 establishes serverless, auto-scaling infrastructure that orqAgent runs. State that the running is ours, in one plain clause. Do not quote the 99.9% uptime figure or any SLA language — that guarantee is Enterprise-only and the brief excludes it — and do not add latency or scale claims the evidence does not carry.

edits.line: upload your handbook files as the agent's knowledge base
edits.problem: "Knowledge base" is a capability noun the evidence does not use and the brief bans twice (do not describe it as a knowledge base product; knowledge base / RAG capability state is unknown). E11 licenses only the literal behaviour: you upload PDFs, docs or plain text and the agent retrieves the most relevant context per query.
edits.fix: Say what the upload does in E11's own terms — the files you upload are what the agent answers from — without naming a knowledge-base or retrieval product category.

edits.line: Point an agent at your own handbook and ask it the questions your team actually asks.
edits.problem: The ask invites an unbounded upload of "your policy docs" (preview text) while the free tier the email is selling caps the knowledge base at five documents. A reader who signs up expecting to load their handbook set and hits that ceiling on the first action loses trust at exactly the moment the email spent everything to reach.
edits.fix: Scope the invitation to what the free tier actually supports — a small, real test on a document or two of their own handbook — so the first session confirms the email rather than contradicting it. Do not state the cap as a limitation headline; make the test small on purpose.

edits.line: The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage.
edits.problem: The mechanics are stated three times before the ask: the preview text (upload, install, it answers), the "write the system prompt, pick the model, upload" paragraph, and this one, whose "no vector DB" half already arrived as "the store behind it stays yours to keep running." That repetition is what pushed the one idea to the bottom of the email where readers had already quit.
edits.fix: Collapse the configuration mechanics into one pass — either this sentence or the preceding one, not both — and give the reclaimed space to the logged-run beat in edit 1.

events.body:
Getting a bot to answer one policy question is the straightforward part.

orqAgent is a no-code platform for building AI agents, and the Slack handbook bot is available now as one of them — configured, not assembled. You write the system prompt, pick the model, and upload your policy documents as PDFs, docs or plain text.

The agent retrieves the most relevant context for every query automatically — no vector DB to manage — and answers from the files you gave it. Slack is an OAuth install; the bot replies to mentions and channel messages.

Every question it answers in the channel is a real agent run. It appears in Analytics exactly like an API call, and Starter keeps a 7-day run history — so the answers going out to the company are on record, not only in the channel.

The running is ours. The platform is serverless and auto-scaling, so there is no pipeline in your name to keep alive after launch week.

> **Starter is $0** — 1,500 free credits, no card required.

Point one agent at your own handbook and ask it the questions your channel actually gets.
